hook: The world’s smallest porpoise lives nowhere else.

story.text: A vaquita surfaces without spectacle: a small grey back, a dark ring around each eye, then water again.
This porpoise lives only in the northern Gulf of California.
Its entire known world is a narrow reach of sea between desert coasts, where sound and touch matter more than sight.
Vaquitas navigate and find food by echolocation, sharing the water with fishing communities whose lives are also bound to the gulf.
The danger is not that vaquitas are hunted.
They become entangled in gillnets, including illegal nets set for totoaba, and cannot return to the surface to breathe.
Research reported by NOAA found no evidence that inbreeding alone makes recovery impossible.
The hopeful condition is also the difficult one: deaths in gillnets must stop.
To witness the vaquita is to remember that disappearance is not abstract.
It is shaped by choices—how fishing is supported, how illegal wildlife trade is confronted, and whether protection in one small sea is made real.

action.title: Understand the threat
action.summary: Read NOAA’s explanation of why gillnets endanger vaquitas and why recovery is still biologically possible.
